q: Which PIDE version (2.x with only α,β vs 3.2+ with raw dose/SF pairs) was used, and does the 318-point NB1RGB count come from raw dose/SF or from re-simulating S = exp(-(αD+βD²)) off the tabulated (α,β)?
basis: The 'random forest RMSE = 0.0196' claim is only interpretable given the underlying variance in the target. If the 318 SF values are re-simulated from smooth (α,β) with no residual scatter, the RF can trivially interpolate and RMSE→0. If they are raw experimental SF with real Poisson-plating scatter, 0.0196 is genuinely striking (and would still be leakage-suspect on a 70/30 point split). Paper §2.1 is ambiguous.
next_steps: Register with GSI PIDE (email form) and download both PIDE 2.2 (α,β only) and PIDE 3.2 (raw dose/SF). Confirm which one gives N=318 for NB1RGB.
Report per-experiment α,β and per-point (dose, SF, LET, experiment_id) so the community can distinguish raw-experimental from re-simulated targets.
Repeat the RF training on both variants and report RMSE separately — if the 'raw' RMSE ≫ 'simulated' RMSE, that quantifies the target-variance issue directly.

q: How does the RF perform under leave-experiment-out (LEO) or leave-cell-line-out (LOCLO) CV, rather than random-point Monte-Carlo CV?
basis: This is the central methodological question. Random-point CV lets the RF see other points from the same experiment (same ion, same LET, same cell state) at training time — it is essentially within-curve interpolation and does not measure what the paper implicitly claims (LET-based prediction of a NEW experiment). A drop from R²≈0.97 → e.g. R²≈0.6 under LEO would completely change the narrative.
next_steps: Reimplement the paper's RF with an sklearn GroupKFold keyed on experiment_id (the paper's own 51-experiment structure supports this natively).
Also run LeaveOneGroupOut over cell lines (using the multi-cell-line PIDE subset the paper mentions in §3.4) — this directly tests transfer to a new biological system.
Report R², RMSE, and per-fold learning curves for both LEO and LOCLO; the delta from random-point MC-CV is the leakage magnitude.

q: How does the RF(dose, LET) compare against a fair physical baseline LQM(α(LET), β(LET)) — i.e., LQ with LET-dependent parameters — rather than dose-only LQ?
basis: The paper's dose-only LQ baseline is a straw man for heavy-ion physics. Everyone in the field knows α and β vary with LET; the Furusawa 2000 NB1RGB curves are decades-old and analytically parameterisable. The RF's 'gain' is largely re-learning those curves empirically. If a physically-informed LQ(α(LET), β(LET)) closes 80% of the gap, the RF's ML value-add collapses to a modest smoothing/interaction term.
next_steps: Fit α(LET) and β(LET) as smooth splines from the training experiments (or use published Furusawa/Weyrather parameterisations), then evaluate LQ(α(LET), β(LET)) on the held-out points.

Also compare against the Microdosimetric Kinetic Model (MKM) with default Kase 2006 parameters and against Repair-Misrepair-Fixation (RMF, Carlson 2008) — these are the standard mechanistic baselines that a claim of 'ML beats classical' should beat.
Report R², RMSE, and residual pattern (RF vs LQ(LET) vs MKM) side-by-side; genuine ML advantage would show up as systematic residual structure that only the RF captures.

q: How does the RF quantify prediction uncertainty, and is that uncertainty calibrated against experimental replicate variance?
basis: The paper reports point predictions and a single RMSE. For clinical / treatment-planning use — which is the paper's motivation — you need per-prediction confidence intervals that are calibrated (e.g., quantile-regression forests, RF infinitesimal jackknife, or conformal prediction). Uncalibrated RF predictions at, say, novel ion species or clinical energies could be catastrophically overconfident precisely where the training data is sparsest.
next_steps: Retrain as a Quantile Regression Forest (or use forestci for RF-IJ variance) to produce 80/95% prediction intervals per point.
Evaluate coverage: fraction of held-out points inside the nominal interval, stratified by LET bin and ion species.
Compare interval width to the experimental replicate scatter in PIDE (where multiple experiments exist for the same (ion, LET, dose)); intervals narrower than replicate scatter are miscalibrated.

q: Does the RF transfer to novel ion species (e.g., helium ions, proton beams at high LET-end-of-range, oxygen) and to clinical energies (100–400 MeV/u for carbon therapy) not densely represented in the training subset?
basis: The training mix is heavily 12C-weighted (24 of 51 experiments) with very few 28Si (7) and 56Fe (5). Clinical hadrontherapy uses primarily protons (LET 0.3–100 keV/µm at end of range) and 12C (LET 10–200 keV/µm). Extrapolation to (a) proton end-of-range LET peaks and (b) space-radiation ion species (Fe at 200+ MeV/u, GCR mix) is where the model would actually be used, and there is no evidence in the paper that it works there.
next_steps: Hold out entire ion species (leave-one-ion-out CV over {C, Ne, Si, Fe}) and report R²/RMSE per held-out ion.
Fetch the proton subset of PIDE (or the PARTNER / NASA GCR datasets) and evaluate the trained RF on those without retraining — the R² drop quantifies out-of-distribution failure.

For clinical energies specifically, compare RF predictions against measured NB1RGB or CHO-K1 survival at HIMAC / GSI / HIT at 200–400 MeV/u, which are outside the training LET density peak; a fair report would include both extrapolation R² and calibration.
